title: Keeping values
question: How do you tell the machine to remember a number?

strengths: You choose the exact place for each value: a register inside the processor, or an address in memory.
You control every byte. A complete DOS program can be smaller than 1 KB.
limits: The 8086 has only eight general registers. You must remember what each one holds.
A value has no type. A byte is only a number until your code gives it a meaning.

example.says: Put the number 100 in register AX.

strengths: Each name has a type, for example INTEGER or REAL. The compiler stops many mistakes before the program runs.
A list or a table of values (an array) is one noun, with a name and a shape.
limits: You do not choose where the values go in memory. The compiler chooses for you.

example.says: Make a whole-number name, lives, with the value 3.

title: Doing arithmetic
question: How do you tell the machine to calculate?

strengths: Each verb is one exact processor step. You know the cost of each step.
Whole-number and fixed-point arithmetic is very fast.
limits: One formula needs many verbs and many registers.
The 8086 has no verbs for decimal-point numbers. It needs an extra maths chip (the 8087) or slow software.

example.code:
mov ax, [speed]
add ax, [boost]
mov [speed], ax
example.says: Make speed equal to speed plus boost. This takes three verbs.

strengths: You write the formula as maths: v = v + a*dt.
Fortran has many ready-made maths idioms, for example SQRT, SIN and ATAN2.
limits: On old hardware without a maths chip, decimal-point arithmetic is slow.

example.says: The same idea in one sentence.

strengths: The grammar is small and clear: compare two values, then jump to a label.
You see each branch that the processor takes.
limits: There is no IF ... ELSE block. A jump to the wrong label is an easy mistake.

example.says: Compare fuel with 0. If they are equal, go to the label no_fuel.

strengths: Choices and loops are blocks: IF ... END IF, SELECT CASE, DO ... END DO. The shape of the text shows the logic.
limits: You do not see the separate steps that the processor does.

example.code:
if (fuel == 0) then
   call no_fuel()
end if
example.says: If fuel is 0, run the subroutine no_fuel.

title: Working with many values
question: How do you do one thing to a long list of values?

strengths: String verbs with the REP adverb copy or fill memory very fast: one sentence, done CX times.
This is the best tool to move screen pixels in a retro game.
limits: You write each loop yourself. There is no ready-made word for sum or average.

example.code:
mov ax, 0A000h
mov es, ax
xor di, di
mov al, 1
mov cx, 64000
rep stosb
example.says: Fill all 64,000 screen pixels with color 1.

strengths: One line does arithmetic on a full array: x = x + v*dt.
Idioms such as SUM, MAXVAL and MATMUL do a full job in one word.
limits: FORTRAN 77, the old dialect of DOS compilers, does not have full-array arithmetic.

example.says: Make every value in the array screen equal to 1.

title: Organizing a program
question: How do you divide a long text into parts with names?

strengths: Labels and macros give names to groups of instructions.
limits: The program is one long list. The language does not enforce a structure. You must keep the order yourself.

example.says: Give the name wait_key to two instructions that wait for a key.

strengths: Modules, subroutines, functions and INTENT keep large programs clear.
The compiler makes sure that each call matches the procedure.
limits: You write more words before the first result.

example.code:
module physics
  implicit none
contains
  pure function next_speed(v, a, dt)
    real, intent(in) :: v, a, dt
    real :: next_speed
    next_speed = v + a*dt
  end function
end module
example.says: A module named physics with one function that calculates the next speed.

title: Showing text and reading keys
question: How does the program talk to the person at the keyboard?

strengths: You call BIOS and DOS services directly: show text, read a key, change the screen mode.
limits: No number formatting. To show a number, you change it to text, one digit at a time.

example.code:
mov ah, 09h
mov dx, msg
int 21h
...
msg db 'Hello$'
example.says: Ask DOS to show the text at msg. The $ marks the end of the text.

strengths: PRINT and WRITE format numbers for you.
The same text works on Linux, macOS and Windows.
limits: Standard Fortran has no words for graphics, sound, or one key press without Enter.

example.says: Show the word Hello on the screen.

title: Controlling the hardware
question: How do you talk to the screen, the keyboard chip and the clock directly?

strengths: This is the native tongue of the processor. Ports, interrupts and screen memory are all in reach.
It is the best tool to make a retro game fast and responsive.
limits: Each processor family speaks a different dialect. 8086 words do not work on an ARM processor.

example.code:
mov dx, 3DAh
vsync: in al, dx
test al, 8
jz vsync
example.says: Wait until the screen beam starts its return to the top (vertical retrace).

strengths: Fortran does not depend on one machine. The same text works on many processors.
limits: Fortran cannot talk to the hardware directly. It needs help from C or from assembly (through ISO_C_BINDING).

example.code:
! Standard Fortran has no word for this.
use iso_c_binding
example.says: Fortran asks a C or assembly routine to do the hardware work.
